<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, we know that this project is the Passbolt open source password manager for teams. It is a full‐stack web application that is built using PHP (with CakePHP conventions visible in the “src/Controller”, “src/Model”, “src/Service”, etc.), and it is organized in a very modular, plugin‐oriented structure. In addition, it supports multiple types of clients (web UI, browser extensions, CLI, mobile app, desktop app) and includes many specialized components for secure authentication (GPG, OpenPGP, JWT, multi‐factor authentication), email notifications, health checks, and more.

Below is our detailed explanation on how to create a precise and comprehensive system design diagram tailored to Passbolt:

1. Identify and Label the Major Components:
  • Clients and User Interfaces:
    - Browser Extensions, Mobile apps, Desktop app (when available) and CLI.
    - Web-based user interface (the “webroot” directory and templates).
  • API/Application Layer:
    - The “src/Controller” and “src/Component” layers expose APIs (HTTP endpoints) that the various clients interact with.
    - This layer implements authentication controllers (AuthLogin, AuthLogout, AuthVerify, etc.) and various domain-specific controllers (Users, Groups, Resources, Secrets).
  • Middleware:
    - A set of middlewares (found under “src/Middleware”) that handle cross-cutting concerns: session management, CSRF protection, SSL enforcement, API versioning, and specific security headers (like GpgAuthHeadersMiddleware).
  • Business Logic / Services Layer:
    - “src/Service” hosts a rich service layer that manages core business logic. For example, separate services to handle authentication tokens, groups, secrets, permissions, resources, password expiry, and the OpenPGP/GPG key processing. There are dedicated services for healthchecks and integration with external systems.
  • Plugin Modules:
    - The “plugins” directory contains multiple plugins such as JWTAuthentication, Folders, EmailDigest, MultiFactorAuthentication and others. Each can be represented as a distinct module that integrates with the overall application.
  • Data Persistence:
    - The “config” files and “src/Model” indicate a robust ORM layer. Your diagram should show a database component (or even multiple databases if applicable) holding the application data (users, groups, resources, keys, etc.).
  • External Infrastructure:
    - Integration points with external systems such as an email server (configured via SMTP settings, see “plugins/PassboltCe/SmtpSettings” and “src/Mailer”), as well as connections for healthchecks.
    
2. Illustrate the Relationships and Data Flows:
  • Show directional arrows from each type of client (web UI, browser extension, mobile app, CLI) to the API layer illustrating incoming HTTP(s) requests.
  • Depict how the API layer calls the middleware for security and request pre-processing before invoking the appropriate business logic in the services layer.
  • Make sure to connect the services layer to the database (for CRUD operations) and to external services such as an email server or third-party integrations.
  • In the diagram, include interactions between the core application and the plugin modules. These modules plug into the main services and extend functionality (for example, the JWTAuthentication plugin influences the authentication flow; the MultiFactorAuthentication plugin adds MFA-related endpoints and middleware).
  
3. Emphasize Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
  • Modular Architecture: The project’s design supports extendability via its plugins, meaning that many features (authentication, logging, localization, password expiry, resource sharing) are implemented as attachable modules.
  • Layered Architecture: There is a clear separation of concerns between the presentation layer (controllers/views), request processing (middleware), business logic (services) and persistence (model/database).
  • Use of Standard Framework Patterns: The project follows conventions typical of CakePHP (such as MVC, use of behaviors on models, and component-based controllers).
  
4. Recommend Diagram Styling and Notation:
  • Use clearly labeled nodes for each major component (for example: "Web Client", "Mobile Client", "Browser Extension", "API Controller", "Middleware", "Business Services", "Plugins", "Database", "External Email Server").
  • Include directional arrows indicating data flow – for instance, from the client to the API, then to middleware (which may modify or validate the request) and onward to services that eventually read from or write to the database.
  • Consider using different shapes or colors to distinguish between layers. For example, use rectangles for application processes, cylinders for databases, and rounded boxes for external integrations.
  • For the plugins, use a grouping (or container) shape that encapsulates the additional functionality and shows how they hook into the main services.
  
5. Tailoring the Diagram to Passbolt’s Domain:
  • Highlight the security-first approach with nodes representing key authentication mechanisms (GPG Authentication, Session Authentication, OpenPGP utilities) and MFA.
  • Emphasize the collaboration aspect by showing a “User / Group Management” component where users can share credentials securely.
  • In the database section, annotate that data entities (Users, Groups, Secrets, Permissions, etc.) are stored centrally.
  • Under “External Infrastructure,” note that healthcheck services and email notifications are vital parts of the system’s operation.
  
6. Additional Diagram Elements:
  • Indicate that the CLI commands (under “src/Command”) are another way to interact with the system, which could be depicted as an alternative client that interacts with the main API layer.
  • Document periodic jobs or scripts that trigger migrations, testing, or scheduled clean-up events (for instance, those in “bin/” or “.gitlab-ci”, which hint at automation and testing infrastructure).
  • Include a legend if you use specific color coding or symbols.
  
By following these guidelines, the system design diagram you produce will capture all the essential layers and components of Passbolt. It will provide a clear overview of how client requests traverse through middleware to invoke business logic and interact with persistence storage, as well as how modular plugins extend and integrate additional functionality.

This detailed, layered diagram will serve as a roadmap of the Passbolt architecture that is both technically precise and visually intuitive for any principal software engineer reviewing the system.
</explanation>
